article_core: The 1892 expedition intervened in an already distributed Harvard-Hosterwitz reference-supply ecology. It moved maker observation into selected American settings while Harvard's existing collection state, season, route, body, time and medium requirements governed what was retained. Botanical references moved in multiple states and on different clocks. Cambridge could externalize gaps and redundancies as selection information; botanical institutions compressed access while wild excursions extended it; returned references became stored workshop stock and were only serially reactivated as identification, priority and capacity allowed. Finished glass then entered a separate chain of mounting, packing, customs, receiving, repair and installation.

gate_B_workshop_reactivation.principle: Retention in 1892 did not imply immediate or eventual glass conversion. Gate B is a queue with latency and competing production programs.

source_critical_guards: No named 1892 Cambridge rejection from the generic already-represented statement.
No HUH search hit is not proof of historical absence.
No exact model string is not proof of no descendant; same genus is not proof of genealogy.
The Harvard >300 herbarium count combines 1892 and 1895.
Promises of later supply are separate from dispatch, receipt, survival, flowering and model reactivation.
Later 1902-1903 collection-state instruments calibrate the mechanism but cannot be projected into 1892 as identical formal paperwork.
Taxonomic latency is documented for some references, not every field object.
Botanical-garden substitution is taxon-specific; the same sources show continuing need for wild excursions.
Darlingtonia batch/shipment timing is closed; direct identity among St Louis sketch, Corning drawing 133264 and physical model 444 remains open.
article_architecture: I. A distributed reference-supply system before and during the journey
II. Gate A: selection by season, collection state, access regime and medium
III. Multiple mobile states and deferred access
IV. Return as inventory: taxonomic, phenological and production latency
V. Gate B: staged reactivation across mixed shipment batches
VI. Finished-object mobility: mounting, freight, customs, unpacking, repair and installation
working_claims: The collection travelled twice: through objects moving to Cambridge and through portable descriptions of what Cambridge still lacked.
The expedition returned as stock, not as a shipment plan.
Fieldwork ended in 1892; the expedition remained operational in the workshop for years.
Botanical gardens compressed botanical access; field excursions extended it.
Transport did not merely move references; it distributed their temporal capacities across different media and institutions.
